Key chemical constituents: essential oil (0.3–1.5%) containing (−)-α-bisabolol, bisabolol oxides A and B, bisabolone oxide A, and (E)-β-farnesene; chamazulene (formed from matricine during steam distillation); flavonoids (apigenin, luteolin, quercetin, patuletin, and their glucosides, notably apigenin-7-glucoside); mucilaginous polysaccharides; coumarins (herniarin, umbelliferone); and phenolic acids.
title: Chamomile (German Chamomile)

text:
Cinnamon (Bark)

Cinnamon bark [Cortex Cinnamomi] is derived from the dried inner bark of Cinnamomum verum and has been used medicinally since antiquity across South Asian, Chinese, and European traditions. Its primary pharmacologically active constituents are trans-cinnamaldehyde, which exerts antimicrobial and antifungal effects by disrupting microbial membrane integrity, and type-A proanthocyanidin polymers, which have been shown in vitro and in small clinical trials to potentiate insulin signalling by up-regulating insulin-receptor kinase activity and inhibiting glycogen synthase kinase-3β. Cinnamaldehyde also produces antispasmodic effects on smooth muscle, supporting traditional use for gastrointestinal complaints such as dyspepsia, flatulence, and mild spasmodic colitis. Anti-inflammatory activity has been documented via inhibition of arachidonic acid metabolism and prostaglandin biosynthesis, which may contribute to analgesic effects observed in traditional use.

Original: Cortex Cinnamomi — Cinnamomum verum J. Presl (syn. C. zeylanicum Blume), family Lauraceae. Principal chemical constituents: volatile oil (1–4%, predominantly trans-cinnamaldehyde 55–90%), cinnamate esters, proanthocyanidins (type-A polymers), diterpenes (cinnzeylanol, cinnzeylanine), coumarin (trace, higher in C. cassia), eugenol (bark oil up to 10%), and polyphenolic polymers with insulin-potentiating activity.
title: Cinnamon (Bark)

text:
Goldthread

Goldthread rhizome (the dried root and rhizome of Coptis chinensis) is used clinically and traditionally to treat gastrointestinal infections, bacterial diarrhoea, and inflammatory conditions of the digestive tract. Its principal active compound, berberine [an isoquinoline alkaloid], exerts broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase and disrupting cell membrane integrity, while also demonstrating anti-inflammatory effects through inhibition of NF-κB signalling and suppression of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Berberine additionally activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), which underlies observed antidiabetic and lipid-lowering effects documented in clinical trials. Traditional pharmacopoeias (Chinese, Japanese, Korean) further record use for fever, conjunctivitis ["red eye"], and oral ulceration, consistent with the plant's antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory profile.

Preparation: DEFINITION: Dried rhizome and fibrous roots of Coptis chinensis Franch. (or C. deltoidea C.Y. Cheng et Hsiao, or C. teeta Wall.), family Ranunculaceae, collected in autumn, cleaned, and dried. BOTANICAL DESCRIPTION: Perennial herb 15–35 cm tall; leaves basal, trifoliate, with deeply incised leaflets; flowers small, white-yellowish; rhizome beaded, bright yellow internally due to berberine content; fibrous roots numerous, forming a "chicken-foot" cluster (Chinese: 鸡爪黄连). GEOGRAPHICAL DISTRIBUTION: Native to mountainous regions of central China (Sichuan, Hubei, Guizhou); cultivated extensively in Sichuan province; related species found in Japan and Himalayan regions. DOSAGE FORMS AND RECOMMENDED DOSES (WHO adult dosage): (1) Dried crude drug (decoction): 1.5–9 g per day in divided doses, prepared as aqueous decoction. (2) Powdered drug (oral): 1–3 g per day. (3) Standardised extract (oral): dose equivalent to 0.9–1.5 g crude drug, taken 2–3 times daily. (4) Berberine hydrochloride tablet (isolated alkaloid): 0.3–0.9 g per day in divided doses for infectious diarrhoea. ADVERSE REACTIONS: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort at high doses; rare hypersensitivity reactions; neonatal haemolytic anaemia and jaundice (bilirubin displacement by berberine — contraindicated in neonates). DRUG INTERACTIONS: May potentiate anticoagulant effects of warfarin; may inhibit CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, increasing plasma levels of co-administered drugs metabolised by these pathways (e.g., cyclosporin, statins). CONTRAINDICATIONS: Pregnancy (uterotonic effects reported in animal studies); neonates and infants (risk of haemolytic jaundice); known hypersensitivity to Coptis species or berberine. Not recommended in cases of deficiency-cold syndromes per traditional Chinese medicine diagnosis.
Indication: Primary conditions (clinical evidence-based): (1) Infectious and non-specific diarrhoea [Clostridium, E. coli, Vibrio cholerae — antimicrobial mechanism]; (2) Type 2 diabetes mellitus [glycaemic control; RCT evidence showing HbA1c reduction comparable to metformin 500 mg TID in several trials]; (3) Dyslipidaemia [LDL-C and triglyceride reduction via PCSK9 inhibition and AMPK activation]; (4) Gastrointestinal inflammation and ulceration [anti-inflammatory, mucosal protective effects]. Traditional uses (pharmacopoeial): fever and heat toxicity syndromes, conjunctivitis, oral ulcers, hypertension.

Original: Rhizoma Coptidis — Coptis chinensis Franch. (Ranunculaceae). Major chemical constituents: berberine (5–8% dry weight), coptisine, palmatine, jatrorrhizine, epiberberine, columbamine, magnoflorine, worenine. Isoquinoline alkaloids predominate, with berberine as the primary pharmacologically active compound.
title: Goldthread

text:
Turmeric

Turmeric (Curcuma longa) is a perennial herb of the ginger family (Zingiberaceae), native to South and Southeast Asia and widely cultivated throughout tropical regions. The medicinal part used is the dried, processed rhizome (underground stem), which is official in numerous national pharmacopoeias. Its principal active constituents are the curcuminoids — chiefly curcumin — which give the rhizome its characteristic deep yellow colour, together with an essential oil fraction rich in sesquiterpene ketones (turmerones). Pharmacologically, curcumin has been demonstrated to inhibit the arachidonic acid cascade (reducing prostaglandin and leukotriene synthesis), to scavenge reactive oxygen species [antioxidant activity], to suppress nuclear factor kappa-B (NF-κB) signalling, and to inhibit platelet aggregation in vitro and in vivo. These mechanisms collectively account for documented anti-inflammatory, hepatoprotective, choleretic [bile-stimulating], carminative [gas-relieving], and antimicrobial effects. Clinical trials support its use as an anti-inflammatory agent comparable in some measures to phenylbutazone and cortisone (without the associated adverse profile), and as a choleretic agent in biliary [gallbladder/bile-duct] dysfunction. Traditional and pharmacopoeial uses additionally include dyspepsia, flatulence, liver complaints, and topical wound healing. Adverse reactions are minimal at recommended doses; prolonged high-dose use may cause gastric irritation. Turmeric is contraindicated in cases of biliary obstruction and should be used with caution in patients with gallstones. No significant drug interactions are established at therapeutic doses, though theoretical interactions with anticoagulants exist given its antiplatelet activity.

Original: Rhizoma Curcumae Longae (Curcuma longa L., Zingiberaceae). Primary chemical constituents: curcuminoids (curcumin, demethoxycurcumin, bisdemethoxycurcumin; collectively 2–9% dry weight of rhizome); volatile oils (4–14%), principally turmerone, atlantone, and zingiberene; polysaccharides (ukonan A–D); fixed oils; resins.
title: Turmeric

text:
Pale Coneflower Root

Pale coneflower root (Echinacea pallida) is used primarily to support the immune system during upper respiratory tract infections, including the common cold and influenza-like illness, by reducing both the severity and duration of symptoms. Its principal pharmacological mechanism is immunomodulation: the caffeic acid derivatives — especially echinacoside — and high-molecular-weight polysaccharides stimulate macrophage activation, enhance phagocytosis, and promote cytokine release (including interferon and interleukin production) in vitro and in vivo. Unlike E. purpurea and E. angustifolia, E. pallida root contains little to no alkylamides, so its immunostimulant activity is attributed chiefly to its echinacoside and polysaccharide fractions. Clinical evidence, including randomised controlled trials, supports a statistically significant reduction in the duration of cold symptoms (mean reduction approximately 1–4 days) when a hydroalcoholic [ethanolic] tincture is administered at onset of illness. Traditional pharmacopoeial use also extends to adjunctive support for chronic infections and superficial wound healing, though evidence for these applications is weaker. Adverse reactions are uncommon at recommended doses; hypersensitivity reactions (including urticaria and, rarely, anaphylaxis) may occur, particularly in individuals with atopic conditions or known allergy to other Asteraceae family members. The plant is contraindicated in progressive systemic diseases such as tuberculosis, leukaemia, collagenosis, multiple sclerosis, and autoimmune disorders, as well as in patients receiving immunosuppressant therapy. Use in pregnancy and lactation is not recommended due to insufficient safety data.

Original: Radix Echinaceae Pallidae — dried root and rhizome of Echinacea pallida (Nutt.) Nutt. (Asteraceae). Key chemical constituents: caffeic acid derivatives (echinacoside, 0.5–1.0% dry weight; 1,3-O-dicaffeoylquinic acid; chlorogenic acid), polyacetylenes (ketoalkenes and ketoalkynes, notably pentadeca-(8Z)-en-2-one), polysaccharides (heteroglycans, arabinogalactans), alkylamides (present in low or trace concentrations, distinguishing E. pallida from E. purpurea and E. angustifolia), and essential oils.
title: Pale Coneflower Root

text:
Purple Coneflower

Purple coneflower (Echinacea purpurea) is a North American prairie herb whose above-ground parts [herba] are used medicinally primarily to support immune function. Clinically, it is best supported as a short-term treatment for reducing the severity and duration of the common cold and upper respiratory tract infections [URTIs], with several randomized controlled trials demonstrating earlier symptom resolution compared to placebo. Pharmacologically, its active constituents — particularly alkylamides and caffeic acid derivatives such as cichoric acid — stimulate macrophage activation, enhance phagocytosis, increase natural killer (NK) cell activity, and promote cytokine production (especially interferon-beta and interleukin-1), thereby amplifying innate immune responses. Polysaccharides and glycoproteins contribute additional immunomodulatory and mild anti-inflammatory effects in vitro and in animal models. Traditional uses extend to wound healing, urinary tract infections, and adjunctive support during bacterial or viral illness, though clinical evidence is strongest for URTI prevention and symptomatic relief. It is contraindicated in individuals with progressive systemic diseases (e.g., tuberculosis, multiple sclerosis, HIV/AIDS, collagen disorders, autoimmune conditions) and in those with known hypersensitivity to Asteraceae plants. It is not recommended for use beyond eight consecutive weeks, as prolonged immunostimulation has not been adequately studied and theoretical immunosuppressive rebound is a concern.

Original: Herba Echinaceae Purpureae — aerial parts of Echinacea purpurea (L.) Moench (Asteraceae), harvested during flowering. Key chemical constituents: caffeic acid derivatives (cichoric acid, up to 2.1%; caftaric acid; chlorogenic acid), alkylamides (isobutylamides of polyunsaturated fatty acids), polysaccharides (heteroxylan, arabinogalactan), glycoproteins, essential oil (humulene, germacrene D), and flavonoids (rutin, quercetin). Echinacoside absent in E. purpurea (characteristic of E. pallida/angustifolia).
title: Purple Coneflower

text:
Ephedra / Ma Huang

Herba Ephedrae consists of the dried young stems (herbaceous aerial parts) of Ephedra sinica Stapf and related species (E. intermedia Schrenk & C.A. Meyer; E. equisetina Bunge), harvested in autumn. The plant is a low-growing, broom-like gymnosperm shrub with scale-like leaves and jointed, green, photosynthetic stems; it is native to arid and semi-arid regions of northern China, Mongolia, and central Asia, and has been cultivated in China for over 5,000 years.

The principal pharmacological activity is attributable to l-ephedrine and d-pseudoephedrine. Ephedrine acts as a sympathomimetic agent through both direct agonism at α- and β-adrenergic receptors and indirect stimulation via norepinephrine release from presynaptic terminals; this dual mechanism produces bronchodilation [relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle via β₂-adrenoceptor activation], vasoconstriction, cardiac stimulation [positive chronotropic and inotropic effects], and central nervous system stimulation. Pseudoephedrine exerts predominantly indirect sympathomimetic effects with somewhat greater selectivity for nasal vasculature, accounting for its use as a nasal decongestant.

Clinical evidence from randomised controlled trials and systematic reviews supports the short-term efficacy of ephedrine and pseudoephedrine as bronchodilators in mild-to-moderate asthma and as nasal decongestants in upper respiratory conditions. A Cochrane-style review of ephedrine in asthma demonstrated statistically significant improvements in forced expiratory volume (FEV₁) and peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) versus placebo, though effect sizes were modest compared to selective β₂-agonists. Studies of ephedrine-containing weight-loss preparations (commonly combined with caffeine) showed short-term reductions in body weight in obese subjects, but with an unfavourable cardiovascular adverse-event profile that substantially limits clinical utility. Traditional pharmacopoeial use in Chinese medicine (recorded in Shennong Bencao Jing, c. 100 CE) includes treatment of asthma [wheezing, dyspnoea], common cold with chills, fever without sweating, oedema, and arthritic pain.

Known adverse reactions include hypertension, tachycardia, palpitations, cardiac arrhythmia, insomnia, nervousness, tremor, headache, urinary retention, and — at high doses or in susceptible individuals — stroke, myocardial infarction, and death. Drug interactions of clinical significance include: monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs; risk of hypertensive crisis), cardiac glycosides (increased risk of arrhythmia), halothane anaesthesia (arrhythmia), guanethidine (antagonism of hypotensive effect), and other sympathomimetic agents (additive toxicity). Contraindications include: hypertension, cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, angle-closure glaucoma, pheochromocytoma, prostatic hyperplasia with urinary retention, anxiety disorders, concurrent MAOI therapy, and pregnancy. Use is contraindicated in children under 12 years. The WHO-recommended adult oral dose of the crude drug is 1.5–9 g per day as a decoction; standardised preparations should be dosed according to alkaloid content, typically providing 15–30 mg total alkaloids per dose, not to exceed three doses daily, and not for use beyond 7 consecutive days without medical supervision.

Original: Herba Ephedrae (Ephedra sinica Stapf, family Ephedraceae). Primary chemical constituents: total alkaloids 1–3% of dry weight, principally l-ephedrine (30–90% of total alkaloid fraction) and d-pseudoephedrine, with minor alkaloids including norephedrine, norpseudoephedrine, methylephedrine, and methylpseudoephedrine. Additional constituents include tannins, flavonoids (including herbacetin glycosides), volatile oils, and polysaccharides.
title: Ephedra / Ma Huang

text:
Ginkgo Leaf

Ginkgo leaf (Folium Ginkgo) is the dried leaf of Ginkgo biloba L., a living-fossil tree native to eastern China and now cultivated globally for both ornamental and medicinal purposes. The leaf is fan-shaped with a distinctive bilobed apex and parallel venation, and it is harvested in autumn from trees that may live over a thousand years. Medicinally, standardised ginkgo leaf extracts are used primarily to treat symptoms of cognitive decline associated with dementia (including Alzheimer's type and multi-infarct dementia), cerebrovascular insufficiency, and peripheral arterial occlusive disease [intermittent claudication]. Pharmacologically, ginkgo's flavonoid fraction acts as a potent free-radical scavenger and antioxidant, protecting neuronal and vascular membranes from oxidative damage, while the terpene trilactones — most critically ginkgolide B — are selective antagonists of platelet-activating factor (PAF), inhibiting platelet aggregation and reducing pathological thrombosis. Together these fractions improve microcirculation, increase cerebral and peripheral blood flow, modulate neurotransmitter systems (including cholinergic and serotonergic pathways), and exert neuroprotective effects demonstrated in both in vitro cell models and in vivo animal studies. Multiple randomised controlled trials (including the landmark 1997 Le Bars et al. JAMA trial, n=309) have documented statistically significant stabilisation or modest improvement in cognitive function and activities of daily living in patients with mild-to-moderate dementia over 26–52 weeks of treatment with standardised EGb 761 extract at 120–240 mg/day, compared to placebo. Adverse reactions are generally mild and include gastrointestinal upset, headache, and allergic skin reactions; rare but serious events include bleeding complications, particularly when used concurrently with anticoagulants (warfarin) or antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel). Ginkgolic acids, present in crude leaf preparations, are contact allergens and potential mutagens, and are reduced to below 5 ppm in pharmaceutical-grade extracts. Ginkgo leaf preparations are contraindicated in known hypersensitivity to Ginkgo biloba preparations, and should be used with caution in patients with coagulation disorders or those taking anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy. The WHO-recommended adult dosage of standardised dry extract (24% flavone glycosides, 6% terpene lactones) is 120–240 mg dry extract per day in two to three divided oral doses; crude leaf preparations and teas are not considered clinically equivalent to standardised extracts and are not recommended for therapeutic use in dementia or vascular indications.

Original: Folium Ginkgo — Ginkgo biloba L. (Ginkgoaceae). Key chemical constituents: flavonoid glycosides (22–27%, principally quercetin, kaempferol, and isorhamnetin glycosides including ginkgoflavone glycosides); terpene trilactones (5–7%, comprising ginkgolides A, B, C, J and bilobalide); biflavones (amentoflavone, bilobetin, ginkgetin, isoginkgetin, sciadopitysin); proanthocyanidins; ginkgolic acids (alkylphenols, kept to <5 ppm in standardised extracts due to potential allergenicity). Standardised dry extract (EGb 761 and LI 1370): 22–27% flavone glycosides, 5–7% terpene lactones.
title: Ginkgo Leaf

text:
Asian Ginseng

Asian ginseng (Panax ginseng) is the dried root of a slow-growing perennial herb native to northeastern China, Korea, and the Russian Far East, long regarded as the pre-eminent tonic herb in East Asian medicine. Its principal bioactive compounds are the triterpenoid saponins collectively called ginsenosides (or panaxosides in Russian literature), which exert a broad range of pharmacological effects including adaptogenic, immunomodulatory, central nervous system-modulating, and antifatigue actions. Clinically, the best-supported uses are as an adaptogen to improve physical and cognitive performance under stress, to support immune function, and as an adjunct in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus (where ginsenosides have demonstrated modest hypoglycaemic effects in randomised controlled trials). Mechanistically, ginsenosides interact with steroid hormone receptors, modulate nitric oxide synthesis, inhibit platelet aggregation, and stimulate natural killer cell and T-lymphocyte activity; individual ginsenosides (e.g., Rb1 vs. Rg1) can exert opposing effects on the central nervous system — sedative/anxiolytic versus stimulant — accounting for the herb's overall balancing or adaptogenic profile.

Preparation: WHO-recommended adult dosage forms and doses: (1) Crude dried root (cut or powdered): 0.5–2 g per day as a decoction or in capsule/tablet form. (2) Standardised dry extract (standardised to ≥4% total ginsenosides): 100–200 mg per day, typically taken in one or two divided doses. (3) Tincture (1:5, 70% ethanol): 2–6 mL per day. General guidance: continuous use is typically recommended for 2–3 month courses, followed by a break of 4–8 weeks before resuming; long-term uninterrupted use is not recommended by WHO. Best taken in the morning or early afternoon to minimise potential stimulant-related sleep disturbance.

Original: Radix Ginseng — Panax ginseng C.A. Meyer (Araliaceae). Principal active constituents: triterpenoid saponins (ginsenosides / panaxosides), comprising approximately 2–3% of dried root by weight, including Rb1, Rb2, Rc, Rd, Re, Rf, Rg1, Rg2, Rh1. Additional constituents include polysaccharides (panaxans), polyacetylenes, peptidoglycans (panaxagins), volatile oils, sterols (beta-sitosterol, stigmasterol), vitamins (B1, B2, B12, C), and the non-saponin fraction containing polyacetylenic alcohols (panaxynol, panaxydol).
title: Asian Ginseng

text:
Siberian Ginseng

Siberian ginseng (Eleutherococcus senticosus) is a thorny shrub native to the Russian Far East, northeastern China, Korea, and Japan, whose dried root and rhizome have been used extensively as an adaptogen [a substance claimed to increase non-specific resistance to biological, chemical, and physical stressors]. Its principal bioactive markers — eleutherosides B and E — are thought to modulate the hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal axis, support immune function via stimulation of T-lymphocytes and natural killer cell activity, and exert mild anti-inflammatory effects through inhibition of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Clinical trials indicate that standardised root extracts (most notably the Soviet-era preparation 'SHE-3', a 33% ethanol extract) can reduce the frequency and severity of herpes simplex type 2 outbreaks, attenuate subjective fatigue and improve physical work capacity in healthy volunteers under stress, and modestly improve cognitive performance in older adults. Evidence for enhancement of athletic performance is mixed and generally not statistically significant in well-controlled studies.

Preparation: WHO-recommended adult dosage (oral, internal use): (1) Dried root/rhizome: 2–3 g per day as a decoction or in capsule/tablet form; (2) Fluid extract (1:1 in 33% ethanol): 2–4 mL three times daily; (3) Solid (dry) extract standardised to ≥1% eleutheroside B+E: 100–200 mg per day; (4) Tincture (1:5 in 40% ethanol): 10–15 mL per day in two to three divided doses. Treatment courses are typically 4–12 weeks; rest periods of 2–3 weeks between courses are traditionally recommended. Preparations should not be taken late in the evening owing to mild stimulant properties.
Indication: Adaptogenic support during periods of physical and mental stress; prophylaxis and reduction of recurrent herpes simplex type 2 outbreaks; supportive treatment of fatigue and debility; adjunct to immune modulation

Original: Radix Eleutherococci — dried roots and rhizomes of Eleutherococcus senticosus (Rupr. & Maxim.) Maxim. (Araliaceae). Key chemical constituents: eleutherosides A–M (principally eleutherosides B [syringin] and E [syringaresinol diglucoside]), polysaccharides (eleutherans A–G), lignans, coumarins, and triterpenoid saponins. Eleutheroside B typically 0.6–0.9% dry weight; eleutheroside E typically 0.6–0.9% dry weight.
title: Siberian Ginseng

text:
Licorice Root

Licorice root (Radix Glycyrrhizae) is the dried root and underground stem (stolon) of Glycyrrhiza glabra and closely related species. Its primary active compound, glycyrrhizin, is a triterpene saponin that inhibits the enzyme 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, thereby potentiating cortisol activity and producing mineralocorticoid-like effects; this underlies both its anti-inflammatory properties and its principal adverse effect (pseudoaldosteronism with sodium retention and hypertension at high or prolonged doses). The flavonoid fraction — particularly glabridin and liquiritigenin — contributes antioxidant, antispasmodic, and mild estrogenic activity, while glycyrrhizinic acid and its metabolite 18β-glycyrrhetinic acid demonstrate antiviral (against Herpes simplex, hepatitis C), hepatoprotective, and mucosal-protective effects documented in both in vitro and animal studies. Clinically, licorice preparations are best supported by evidence for use as an expectorant and demulcent in upper respiratory tract irritation and catarrh, and as a gastrointestinal antispasmodic and anti-ulcer agent, including adjunctive use in peptic ulcer disease (particularly the deglycyrrhizinated form, DGL, which retains mucosal-protective benefit with reduced systemic hormonal risk).

Original: Radix Glycyrrhizae — dried, unpeeled or peeled root and stolon of Glycyrrhiza glabra L. (Fabaceae), or related species G. uralensis Fisch. and G. inflata Bat. Major chemical constituents: triterpene saponins (glycyrrhizin / glycyrrhizinic acid, 2–25% by dry weight, typically ~4–6% in pharmacopoeial material); aglycone 18β-glycyrrhetinic acid (enoxolone); flavonoids and isoflavonoids (liquiritin, isoliquiritin, liquiritigenin, formononetin, glabridin); coumarins (glycycoumarin, glabrocoumarone); polysaccharides; phytosterols (β-sitosterol, stigmasterol); volatile oils (trace). Glycyrrhizin is approximately 50× sweeter than sucrose.
title: Licorice Root

text:
Goldenseal

Goldenseal rhizome is used clinically and traditionally as an antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and mucous-membrane tonic. Its principal alkaloid, berberine, inhibits bacterial adherence to epithelial cells, disrupts microbial cell membranes, and modulates intestinal secretion, providing a mechanistic basis for its use in gastrointestinal infections and diarrhoea. Hydrastine exerts vasoconstrictive and uterotonic effects via adrenergic pathways, while canadine contributes smooth-muscle relaxation and mild sedative activity. Together, these alkaloids support the plant's traditional applications in catarrhal inflammation of mucosal surfaces — including the upper respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, and genitourinary tract — as well as its use as a haemostatic agent in postpartum haemorrhage. Clinical evidence is limited but includes positive findings for berberine-containing preparations in infectious diarrhoea (including cholera and giardiasis) and modest supportive data for upper respiratory tract infections; evidence specific to the whole rhizome preparation remains sparse, and most pharmacological data derive from isolated berberine studies.

Preparation: WHO-referenced adult dosage forms: (1) Dried rhizome/root: 0.5–1 g as decoction or infusion three times daily. (2) Liquid extract (1:1 in 60% ethanol): 0.3–1 ml three times daily. (3) Tincture (1:10 in 60% ethanol): 2–4 ml three times daily. (4) Powdered solid extract (standardised to ≥5% total alkaloids or ≥2.5% berberine): 250–500 mg per dose. Topical: dilute preparations applied to mucous membranes as an astringent wash. Duration of use should not exceed 3 weeks continuously without medical supervision.
Indication: Infectious diarrhoea (including traveller's diarrhoea, cholera adjunct, giardiasis); catarrhal inflammation of upper respiratory mucosa; mucosal antisepsis (oral, gastrointestinal, genitourinary); topical wound care and conjunctivitis (traditional/limited evidence); uterine haemorrhage (historical/traditional use only — not recommended in modern clinical practice due to uterotonic risk)

Original: Rhizoma Hydrastis — dried rhizome and roots of Hydrastis canadensis L. (Ranunculaceae). Principal active constituents: isoquinoline alkaloids, primarily berberine (2–4% dry weight), hydrastine (1.5–4%), canadine (l-tetrahydroberberine; trace–1%), and berberastine; additionally hydrastinine (oxidative degradation product of hydrastine), resin, meconine, and volatile oil. Total alkaloid content typically 3.5–6% by dry weight.
title: Goldenseal

text:
St. John's Wort

St. John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum) is a perennial herbaceous plant whose dried aerial flowering parts [Herba Hyperici] have well-documented antidepressant activity supported by multiple randomised controlled trials and systematic reviews. Its principal mechanisms of action include inhibition of synaptic reuptake of serotonin, dopamine, noradrenaline, GABA, and L-glutamate — an effect attributed primarily to hyperforin — as well as downregulation of beta-adrenergic receptors and upregulation of serotonin receptor density with prolonged use. Hypericin and pseudohypericin additionally exert antiviral activity in vitro (including against HIV and influenza), while the flavonoid and phloroglucinol fractions contribute anti-inflammatory and anxiolytic effects. Clinically, standardised extracts of Herba Hyperici have demonstrated efficacy superior to placebo and broadly comparable to standard tricyclic antidepressants in mild-to-moderate depression, with a more favourable short-term tolerability profile. Traditional and pharmacopoeial uses extend to topical application for wound healing, burns, neuralgia, and mild anxiety, and oral use for menopausal mood disturbance and seasonal affective disorder. Significant pharmacokinetic herb–drug interactions occur via induction of cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP3A4, CYP2C9) and P-glycoprotein, reducing plasma levels of co-administered drugs including ciclosporin, antiretrovirals, oral contraceptives, digoxin, and warfarin.

Preparation: ORAL (internal use): Dried herb infusion: 2–4 g dried herb in 150 ml boiling water, 3 times daily. Dry extract (standardised to 0.3% hypericins): 300 mg, 3 times daily (total 900 mg/day); most widely studied dose in clinical trials. Fluid extract (1:1 in 25% ethanol): 2–4 ml, 3 times daily. Tincture (1:10 in 45% ethanol): 2–4 ml, 3 times daily. TOPICAL (external use): Semi-solid preparations containing 0.2–1.0% hypericin-equivalent extract applied to affected area as needed for minor wounds, mild burns, and myalgia. NOTE: Full antidepressant effect typically requires 4–6 weeks of continuous use at therapeutic dose.

Original: Herba Hyperici — Hypericum perforatum L. (Hypericaceae). Key chemical constituents: naphthodianthrone derivatives (hypericin, pseudohypericin; total hypericins ~0.03–0.3% dry weight), phloroglucinols (hyperforin, adhyperforin; hyperforin ~2–4% dry weight), flavonoids (hyperoside, rutin, quercetin, isoquercitrin, amentoflavone), biflavones, xanthones, phenolic acids (chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid), volatile oils, and tannins (proanthocyanidins).
title: St. John's Wort

text:
Peppermint Leaf

Peppermint leaf [Folium Menthae Piperitae] is the dried or fresh leaf of Mentha x piperita L., a hybrid mint of the family Lamiaceae. Its primary pharmacological activity is driven by the volatile essential oil, chiefly menthol, which acts as a selective kappa-opioid receptor agonist and calcium channel antagonist on intestinal smooth muscle, producing antispasmodic and carminative effects; menthol also activates TRPM8 cold-thermoreceptors in peripheral sensory neurons, producing the characteristic cooling sensation used in topical analgesic and antipruritic applications. Clinically, enteric-coated peppermint oil capsules have demonstrated efficacy in reducing the frequency and severity of symptoms in Irritable Bowel Syndrome [IBS] in multiple randomised controlled trials, and inhalation or topical application of diluted peppermint oil has shown benefit for tension-type headache and nausea. Rosmarinic acid and other phenolic constituents contribute antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial properties documented in in vitro studies.

Original: Folium Menthae Piperitae — Mentha x piperita L. (Lamiaceae). Key chemical constituents: essential oil (1.0–3.0% in fresh leaf, up to 4.0% dried), composed primarily of menthol (35–55%), menthone (10–35%), menthyl acetate (3–10%), menthofuran (1–10%), 1,8-cineole (eucalyptol, 3–8%), and isomenthone (2–10%); also contains flavonoids (luteolin, menthoside, rutin, hesperidin), phenolic acids (rosmarinic acid, caffeic acid), and triterpenes (ursolic acid, oleanolic acid).
title: Peppermint Leaf

text:
Peppermint Oil

Peppermint oil is the steam-distilled volatile oil obtained from the fresh flowering aerial parts of the hybrid mint Mentha x piperita (family Lamiaceae). Its dominant constituent, menthol, activates cold-sensitive TRPM8 receptors in sensory neurons, producing the characteristic cooling sensation and exerting local anaesthetic, antispasmodic, and mild analgesic effects. Clinically, enteric-coated capsules of the oil relax smooth muscle of the gastrointestinal tract by blocking calcium influx, reducing colonic spasm and pain; this mechanism is supported by multiple randomised controlled trials demonstrating efficacy in Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS). Applied topically, a 10% ethanolic solution of peppermint oil has been shown in controlled trials to be as effective as paracetamol (acetaminophen) in relieving tension-type headache when applied to the forehead and temples. The oil also exhibits in vitro antimicrobial and antiviral activity, and inhalation preparations are used traditionally to relieve symptoms of upper respiratory catarrh by promoting nasal airflow and loosening mucus secretions [mucolytic/decongestant action].

Preparation: ORAL (IBS/gastrointestinal spasm): Enteric-coated capsules of 0.2–0.4 mL peppermint oil, taken three times daily between meals (total daily dose 0.6–1.2 mL). Enteric coating is essential to prevent premature release in the stomach, which causes oesophageal sphincter relaxation and heartburn. TOPICAL (tension headache): 10% ethanolic solution of peppermint oil applied liberally to forehead and temples at headache onset; may reapply at 15–30 minute intervals up to three times. INHALATION (nasal congestion/catarrh): A few drops added to hot water for steam inhalation, or applied as a semi-solid nasal ointment/rub to the chest or below the nostrils; commercial lozenges and sprays also used. TOPICAL (myalgia/neuralgia): Oil or creams containing ≥10% menthol applied to affected areas. NOTE: Products intended for use in or near the faces of infants and children under 2 years are contraindicated. Doses above are for adults.
Indication: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS); gastrointestinal spasm and flatulence; tension-type headache (topical); symptoms of common cold and upper respiratory catarrh (inhalation); musculoskeletal pain and pruritis (topical)

Original: Aetheroleum Menthae Piperitae — Essential oil distilled from the fresh aerial parts of Mentha x piperita L. (Lamiaceae). Principal constituents: menthol (29–48%), menthone (20–31%), menthyl acetate (3–10%), menthofuran (1–9%), 1,8-cineole (3–6%), isomenthone, neomenthol, and menthyl isovalerate. The oil must conform to pharmacopoeial standards for specific gravity, optical rotation, refractive index, and content of total esters calculated as menthyl acetate.
title: Peppermint Oil

text:
Kava

Kava is a Pacific Island shrub whose dried rhizome [underground stem] has been used ceremonially and medicinally for centuries across Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia. The plant's active compounds — collectively called kavalactones or kavapyrones — act on the central nervous system [CNS] through multiple mechanisms: modulation of gamma-aminobutyric acid [GABA-A] receptors (enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission), blockade of voltage-gated sodium and calcium ion channels, inhibition of noradrenaline [norepinephrine] reuptake, reversible inhibition of monoamine oxidase B [MAO-B], and reduction of excitatory glutamate transmission. These combined actions produce anxiolytic [anxiety-reducing], sedative, muscle-relaxant, and mild analgesic effects without, at therapeutic doses, causing significant cognitive impairment or dependence of the classic benzodiazepine type. Clinical trial evidence — including several randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies and at least one systematic meta-analysis (notably Pittler & Ernst, 2000) — supports the efficacy of standardised kava extract (typically standardised to 70% kavalactones by the WS 1490 preparation) for the treatment of non-psychotic anxiety disorders, with statistically significant reductions on the Hamilton Anxiety Scale [HAMA] versus placebo. Traditional uses extend to promotion of sleep, relief of urinary tract infections, management of menopausal symptoms, and topical analgesia for toothache and mouth sores. Safety concerns centre on rare but serious hepatotoxicity [liver toxicity], which has led regulatory agencies in multiple countries to restrict or suspend kava-containing products; the mechanism of hepatotoxicity is debated but may involve toxic alkaloids concentrated in aerial plant parts, cytochrome P450 [CYP] enzyme inhibition, and/or idiosyncratic immune reactions. Use of the root or rhizome only — excluding stems and leaves — and avoidance of alcohol co-ingestion are considered important risk-mitigation factors.

Preparation: RECOMMENDED DOSAGE FORMS AND DOSES (WHO Monographs, adult use only): (1) Standardised dry extract (acetone/water extraction, standardised to 70% kavalactones; e.g., WS 1490): 100 mg extract three times daily, equivalent to approximately 210 mg total kavalactones per day; course duration generally not to exceed 3 months without medical supervision. (2) Aqueous extract (traditional water-based preparation): equivalent to 60–120 mg kavalactones per day, divided doses. (3) Ethanolic extract preparations: dose standardised to provide no more than 250 mg kavalactones per day per WHO guidance. IMPORTANT: Preparations derived exclusively from the peeled, dried rhizome/root; aerial plant parts (stems, leaves) must be excluded. Prolonged use beyond 4–8 weeks should occur only under physician oversight with periodic liver function monitoring. NOT for use in conjunction with alcohol, benzodiazepines, barbiturates, or other CNS depressants.
Indication: Anxiety disorders (non-psychotic); generalised anxiety; nervous tension and restlessness [traditional]; insomnia associated with anxiety; menopausal anxiety and irritability

Original: Rhizoma Piperis Methystici — Piper methysticum G. Forst. (Piperaceae). Primary chemical constituents: kavalactones (kavapyrones), comprising 3–20% of dry rhizome weight, including kavain (kawain), dihydrokavain, methysticin, dihydromethysticin, yangonin, and desmethoxyyangonin. Additional constituents include chalcones (flavokavains A, B, C), pipermethystine (a piperidine alkaloid found chiefly in aerial parts), starch (~43%), proteins, and minerals.
title: Kava

text:
Psyllium (Blond Psyllium / Isabgol)

Psyllium (blond psyllium, isabgol) consists of the dried ripe seeds and/or husks of Plantago ovata, a small annual herb native to South Asia and the Mediterranean. The husk is extraordinarily rich in mucilaginous arabinoxylans — soluble, gel-forming dietary fibers — which are the primary pharmacologically active fraction. Upon contact with water, these polysaccharides swell to form a viscous gel in the gastrointestinal lumen. In the context of constipation and bowel regularity, this bulk-forming mechanism softens stool, increases fecal mass, and promotes peristalsis, reducing intestinal transit time without stimulating the mucosa directly. For hypercholesterolaemia, the viscous gel binds bile acids in the small intestine, interrupting enterohepatic circulation and compelling the liver to convert additional cholesterol to bile acids, thereby reducing serum LDL-cholesterol [low-density lipoprotein cholesterol] by approximately 5–15% in controlled trials. Secondary effects on postprandial blood glucose and insulin response have been documented, attributable to slowed gastric emptying and reduced carbohydrate absorption rate. Clinical trials and systematic reviews support psyllium's efficacy as a bulk-forming laxative in chronic idiopathic constipation, irritable bowel syndrome with constipation (IBS-C), and as an adjunctive lipid-lowering agent. Traditional and pharmacopoeial uses extend to management of diarrhoea (where the gel matrix absorbs excess luminal fluid and normalises stool consistency), haemorrhoids, and as a food supplement to improve glycaemic control in type 2 diabetes mellitus. The drug is generally well tolerated; the principal adverse reactions are flatulence, bloating, and, rarely, IgE-mediated [immunoglobulin E-mediated] allergic hypersensitivity (including occupational asthma in healthcare workers handling psyllium powder). Psyllium should not be administered to patients with known hypersensitivity to Plantago species, esophageal narrowing or any gastrointestinal obstruction, or to patients who are unable to swallow safely or maintain adequate fluid intake. It may delay oral absorption of concurrently administered drugs (notably lithium, carbamazepine, digoxin, warfarin, and certain antidiabetic agents) and should be taken separately from other medications by at least one to two hours.

Preparation: WHO-recommended adult dosage: Bulk-forming laxative and bowel regulator — 7–11 g whole or ground seed (or 4–6 g husk) dissolved or stirred into a full glass (≥200–250 mL) of water or other liquid, administered 1–3 times daily before meals, followed immediately by an additional glass of liquid. Lipid-lowering indication — 10–20 g/day total psyllium husk, typically divided into two or three doses with meals, incorporated into food or taken as a suspension; minimum 4–8 week treatment period required to assess lipid response. Dosage forms: oral powder/granules for suspension; capsules (as husk); wafers; psyllium-enriched food products. Paediatric dosing (>6 years): half the adult dose with proportionally increased fluid; not recommended in children under 6 years without medical supervision. Critical administration instruction: always take with a full glass of water; inadequate fluid intake risks esophageal or intestinal obstruction.
Indication: 1. Chronic idiopathic constipation (bulk-forming laxative, first-line non-pharmacological agent). 2. Irritable bowel syndrome with constipation [IBS-C] (reduces stool hardness and improves bowel frequency). 3. Hypercholesterolaemia / dyslipidaemia (adjunctive LDL-cholesterol lowering; FDA-approved health claim for cardiovascular disease risk reduction). 4. Type 2 diabetes mellitus — adjunctive management of postprandial hyperglycaemia. 5. Diarrhoea — symptomatic normalisation of stool consistency (traditional and pharmacopoeial use). 6. Haemorrhoids — softening stool to reduce straining (traditional use, supported by guidelines).

Original: Semen Plantaginis — Plantago ovata Forssk. (Plantaginaceae). Key chemical constituents: mucilaginous polysaccharides (husk: 10–30% of seed weight, composed chiefly of arabinoxylans); fixed oils (5–10%); iridoid glycosides (aucubin); proteins (~15–20%); tannins; flavonoids (luteolin, apigenin derivatives); phytosterols (beta-sitosterol, campesterol). The pharmaceutical material is the dried, ripe seed and/or the separated seed husk (psyllium husk / ispaghula husk).
title: Psyllium (Blond Psyllium / Isabgol)
